findings.title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
findings.body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` makes the default value a class-level constant computed when the module is first imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` (which never passes `queued`) will therefore carry the process start/import timestamp, which can be hours or days stale. Any present or future logic that reasons about how long ago the assignment was queued (e.g. expiring the cycle-breaking context) will be silently wrong, and the field's value is misleading in logs/payloads. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

findings.title: `to_dict`/`from_dict` do not survive a Celery JSON round-trip with a typed `queued`
findings.body: `to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, so `queued` is a raw `datetime` that is handed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={... "assignment_source_dict": ...})`. Celery/kombu's JSON serializer will encode it as an ISO-8601 string (and a stricter serializer would reject it outright), and `from_dict` simply does `cls(**input_dict)` with no coercion, so the reconstructed object's `queued` is a `str` even though it is annotated `datetime`. Anything that later compares or arithmetics on `queued` will raise `TypeError` at runtime. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()`) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

findings.title: Malformed assignment source is silently dropped, re-enabling sync cycles
findings.body: `from_dict` swallows `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`. In `sync_assignee_outbound` the returned `None` is passed to `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)`, which means the cycle-prevention check is skipped entirely and the change is propagated back to the originating integration — exactly the loop this PR is meant to break. Since this failure mode is invisible (no log, no metric), a payload-shape change (e.g. the `queued` serialization issue above, or an added/renamed field during a deploy) would silently reintroduce the sync loop. Log/capture the parse failure instead of returning `None` silently.

findings.title: `sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter that is never passed or implemented
findings.body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller passes it (the status-sync task still calls `sync_status_outbound(external_issue, is_resolved, project_id)`), no concrete integration implementation was updated, and `should_sync("outbound_status")` is still invoked without a source. The parameter is dead API surface that suggests status sync cycles are now broken when they are not; subclasses that only accept `**kwargs` would silently swallow the argument if someone starts passing it. Either wire the status path through (task kwarg + `should_sync` call + implementations) or drop the parameter from this signature.

findings.title: New positional second argument to `should_sync` can break duck-typed installations
findings.body: The task only checks `hasattr(installation, "should_sync")` and now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with two positional arguments. Any installation class that defines `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-argument signature (only the two definitions in `mixins/issues.py` were updated here) will now raise `TypeError`, which the `@retry` decorator will retry 5 times before giving up — silently breaking outbound assignee sync for that provider. Additionally the parameter is named `sync_source` in `should_sync` but `assignment_source` everywhere else, so keyword calls will not be interchangeable; align the names and verify no other `should_sync` overrides exist.

findings.title: No test covers the dict round-trip or the per-instance `queued` default
findings.body: The new tests only assert that `to_dict()["queued"]` is not `None` and that `from_dict` works for a dict without `queued`. They never (a) assert that `queued` differs between two instances created at different times, which would have caught the import-time default evaluation bug, nor (b) round-trip `to_dict()` through JSON serialization and back into `from_dict`, which is exactly how the value travels in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Both the real failure modes of this dataclass are therefore untested.

findings.title: Cycle-breaking is only tested for assign, not deassign, and never through the task boundary
findings.body: There is a new test for `assign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` not triggering outbound sync, but no equivalent test for `deassign(..., assignment_source=...)`, even though `sync_group_assignee_inbound` now passes a source on the unassign path. Also, all tests run under `self.tasks()` (eager execution), so `assignment_source_dict` is handed to the task as a live `dict` with a `datetime`; the serialize/deserialize path used in production (and therefore `AssignmentSource.from_dict` receiving a string `queued`) is never exercised. A regression in that path would silently restore the sync loop without failing any test.
